title: 25 Questions to Ask During 2x10s
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This is a practical companion piece to Stuart's earlier writing on 2x10s, the two-minutes-for-ten-days relationship-building strategy for reaching disengaged or difficult students. Rather than re-explaining the strategy, he supplies a ready-to-use bank of conversation-starter questions for teachers who freeze up when facing a resistant student and don't know where to begin. He illustrates the method with a story about a student named Ruby, showing how a teacher works through several questions until one produces a genuine spark, then follows that thread across subsequent conversations rather than defaulting back to generic small talk. The larger point is that 2x10s succeed not from the specific topic covered but from a teacher's sustained, authentic interest in something the student already values, and that this shared territory becomes the basis of the student's association with the teacher and, by extension, the class.
points: The question bank functions as an entry-point toolkit for teachers who know the 2x10 strategy in theory but struggle in practice to start a conversation with a resistant student.

Stuart's Ruby example demonstrates the strategy's real mechanism: work through questions until one produces a "spark," then keep mining that specific thread in later conversations rather than starting from scratch each time.

The underlying claim is that what makes 2x10s work isn't the topic itself but sustained authentic curiosity, which becomes the basis for a student associating the teacher with something they genuinely value.
quotes: I've written and spoken before about 2x10s. If you're not familiar with the strategy, either read this quick article or watch the quick video below.
But something I've never done is give a list of prompts you can use to start eliciting conversation from these challenging kinds of students.
Sometimes, I need to work through a handful of these before I sense a spark in a student's eyes. When I sense that, I keep asking more questions along that spark-inducing thread.

I once had a student named Ruby who didn't much want to talk to me during 2x10s, until I asked her about TV shows. Her response made it clear she liked this topic. In subsequent 2x10s, I started asking her for show recommendations.
I didn't have time to watch these shows, but I did make a note to watch the trailer or a clip on YouTube and let her know what I thought.

The key with 2x10s is to just gain some ground somewhere, anywhere, that a student authentically values. Keep exploring that territory, and as the days add up, the student will start associating you not just with the class you teach but also with this thing they value.
